title: Bram and the Static
premise: Jonah Pemberton has spent eleven years alone on the terraforming station Verdance, tending a garden for colonists who will never arrive and maintaining a beacon whose original orders were lost in the war. When the deep-space vessel Halcyon returns with its crew aged backward into children, carrying a message that could end the decades-long war between Earth and the Outer Colonies, Jonah becomes the last adult who can decode and deliver it. Hunted by both sides and betrayed by the one ally she trusted, she must choose between preserving her invisibility and sacrificing herself to broadcast the truth — discovering that the beacon she tended was built for exactly this moment by the woman she once loved. In the end, Jonah delivers the message at the cost of Verdance itself, and the found family of regrown crew members carries her legacy into a fragile peace.
about_author: Hazel Eastwick is the pen name of a former hydroponics technician who spent six years on orbital agricultural stations before turning to fiction. She writes quiet, character-driven science fiction about people who keep things running while history happens elsewhere.

chapters.title: The Garden for No One
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A day in the rhythm of Verdance: pruning gene-tweaked wheat, logging weather, resetting the beacon on its 40-hour cycle. Through small details we learn the war ended her supply runs years ago. Emotional beat: loneliness worn so smooth it feels like peace — until the sky splits with an incoming ship.

chapters.title: Halcyon
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A battered deep-space vessel makes an unpowered landing in her fields. The crew who emerges are children — biologically reversed, memories fragmentary. Their captain, now nine years old, presses a data core into Jonah's hands and says only: 'It has to go back.' Emotional beat: wonder curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Children of the Long Dark
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, intercut with young Captain Ilsa Reyes's fragmented memories. The children remember being old; their bodies disagree. Jonah realizes the reversal is a weapon test gone wrong — or right. Emotional beat: reluctant responsibility as she counts mouths she cannot feed.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Hears
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Examining the data core, she finds it interfaces with her beacon — hardware she thought obsolete suddenly resonating. Embedded logs reveal the beacon predates the war and was commissioned under a name she recognizes: Dr. Amara Voss, the scientist who trained her. Emotional beat: the past reaching through machinery.

chapters.title: Two Flags on the Horizon
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Both warring factions have detected Halcyon's return. Scout drones circle Verdance. Ilsa, inhabiting a child's body but a commander's mind, argues they must move the core before someone arrives to take it. Emotional beat: two kinds of stubbornness finding grudging respect.

chapters.title: The Man from Supply
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. An Earth supply ship lands with 'relief aid' and Officer Dain Corrick, who knew Jonah before she vanished into terraforming service. He offers extraction — for her alone. The children would be 'quarantined.' Emotional beat: temptation, and the first crack in her invisibility.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, flashback-heavy. Why she chose exile: she testified against Voss's weapons research and then ran from what her testimony unleashed. The beacon was Voss's gift, or her trap. Emotional beat: guilt as architecture — every wall she built named after something she fled.

chapters.title: Quarantine
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Corrick's marines begin 'screening' the children; two are sedated and loaded for transport. Ilsa organizes the others using games as cover. Jonah must decide whether her comfortable lie is worth more than thirty small lives. Emotional beat: the moment complicity becomes impossible.

chapters.title: Cutting the Tether
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. She sabotages the transport shuttle and confronts Corrick, burning her last bridge to Earth. They flee to the beacon array with the core. Emotional beat: terror and exhilaration — the first choice she's made in a decade that costs her something.

chapters.title: Voss's Voice
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The core unlocks against the beacon, playing a recorded message from Amara Voss: the reversal effect is real, repeatable, and the message inside is proof of a war crime both sides committed — a plague seeded on a colony ship. Delivering it ends the war; suppressing it protects whoever holds it. Emotional beat: grief for a mentor who weaponized her.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Survival
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The children debate: give the message to the Outer Colonies (their origin) and risk Earth destroying Verdance, or trade it back to Earth for amnesty. Ilsa refuses to be currency again. Emotional beat: children forced to think like generals, and what that steals from them.

chapters.title: Signal Ghosts
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Both fleets are inbound. The beacon can broadcast planet-wide — once — before Earth jamming kills it permanently. But broadcasting also reveals Verdance's location to everyone. Jonah starts prepping the garden for evacuation, transplanting seedlings into mobile racks. Emotional beat: tenderness toward living things as rehearsal for letting go.

chapters.title: Corrick's Bargain
chapters.summary: Corrick's POV. Not a monster — a loyal man who believes the message must never air, because he's seen what truth did to the last ceasefire. He offers Jonah a deal: her silence in exchange for the children's safe passage home. Emotional beat: an antagonist who is almost right, which is worse.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Ensemble scene, Ilsa presiding. The children vote on the message's fate. A boy named Teo, the youngest, asks the question that breaks the deadlock: 'If nobody tells, does it happen again?' The vote: broadcast. Emotional beat: democracy among the damaged, and dignity in small voices.

chapters.title: Jamming
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Earth ships enter orbit and begin jamming. The beacon needs forty minutes of clear window; the fleet will give them four. Ilsa proposes using Halcyon itself as a relay decoy. Preparations take on funeral weight. Emotional beat: clock-tight dread, hands steady anyway.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Array
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. One of the older children, Renn, has been transmitting to Corrick — not for money, but because his regrown body is failing and Earth promised treatment. He takes the core. Jonah catches him at the shuttle pad. Emotional beat: heartbreak over anger; even betrayal is a kind of survival.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dying
chapters.summary: Jonah and Renn's shared scene. She doesn't stop him — she goes with him, trading herself for the core's return, buying time while Ilsa reroutes the broadcast through Halcyon. Emotional beat: mercy as strategy; the price of survival paid in person.

chapters.title: Forty Minutes
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV, climax part one. With Jonah captive aboard Corrick's ship, Ilsa leads the children through the broadcast sequence as jamming closes in. Halcyon rises as a decoy and takes fire. The window opens. Emotional beat: children doing an adult's impossible work, terrified and precise.

chapters.title: The Message
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, climax part two. On Corrick's bridge, she forces him to listen to Voss's recording as it airs planet-wide — the crime, the names, the proof. Crewmen lower their weapons one by one. Corrick doesn't stop the broadcast; he stops his own fleet's retaliation order. Emotional beat: catharsis — truth as detonation and release.

chapters.title: Ash and Seedlings
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the ceasefire chaos, Verdance burns — whether by accident or spite is never determined. Jonah walks the ruined garden, salvaging what she can. Renn dies aboard the medical ship, his confession included in the record. Emotional beat: mourning that refuses to become regret.

chapters.title: The Ones Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Peace talks convene; the children are witnesses, not bargaining chips, because Jonah insisted. Some crew choose repatriation; Ilsa and seven others stay with Jonah. They break ground on a new garden together. Emotional beat: found family chosen in the wreckage, tentative and real.

chapters.title: Beacon, Rebuilt
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, coda. One year later: a working settlement, a school, a new beacon — this one commissioned openly, its purpose written down where no one can lose it. Jonah teaches the children botany and signal theory. Final line echoes chapter one's routine, transformed. Emotional beat: survival was the price; this is what it bought.
